content:
Why Another Tech Blog? I have been thinking about this little project for a while, and after the usual procrastination, I finally got started on it. With the help of my trusty assistant, ChatGPT, I got this site up and running in no time.
Like a lot of projects I start, they can sometimes get abandoned and forgotten about. Let’s see what happens to this one.
What Will Be Here Soon? Hopefully, my ramblings with a bit of useful stuff thrown in. Mostly my homelab stuff and anything else I happen to be tinkering with.
I am predominantly a Linux and open-source user, so it will usually be tied in with that. I also love the Raspberry Pi ecosystem. I know they are expensive at the moment, but I live in a caravan (grey nomad), so being able to run stuff on 12V is a must.
To get things started, my first guide is about how I built this site with Hugo and PaperMod, put it on GitHub and deployed it automatically using Cloudflare Workers.
Here is the link Deploy a Hugo Site to Cloudflare

title: Starting Vincatech

content:
Today I decided to set up a small tech blog using Hugo. I wanted something simple, Markdown files, which are my favourite format these days for all things notes, good SEO, no point having a website if no one can find it and very little maintenance, and automatic deployment whenever I push changes to GitHub.
I settled on the PaperMod theme and decided to use GitHub for the repository, with Cloudflare for hosting. PaperMod met all my requirements as far as SEO was concerned, and it looked like a simple theme, which for me means that if I want to make changes, I can without having to kill myself reading documentation.
Prerequisites This guide assumes:
You can get Hugo working on your computer. Your Hugo site will be stored in a GitHub repository. You have a Cloudflare account. Your domain is already using Cloudflare for DNS. In my case, vincatech.net was already managed by Cloudflare, so Cloudflare could configure the DNS for the Worker when I added it as a Custom Domain.
When all is in place the final work flow below should be largely automatic, other than me writing the article and then git push everything else should just work.
Write article ↓ git push to Github ↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓ Automatic Cloudflare ↓ Hugo build ↓ Cloudflare Worker ↓ vincatech.net Installing Hugo I’m using Fedora, which already had a recent extended version of Hugo available, the following commands got me started.
sudo dnf install hugo hugo version --> hugo v0.162.1+extended linux/amd64 cd ~ hugo new site vincatech cd vincatech git init git submodule add https://github.com/adityatelange/hugo-PaperMod.git themes/PaperMod rm hugo.toml nvim hugo.yml hugo.yml baseURL: "https://vincatech.net/" locale: "en-AU" title: "VincaTech" theme: "PaperMod" enableRobotsTXT: true params: env: production description: "Tech notes, projects and ideas." author: "Vincent" ---- For search ---- outputs: home: - HTML - RSS - JSON To check what the state of play is, try the following command -
hugo server -D The -D means development which includes draft articles.
Organising the Content I decided on three main types of content:
Posts for dated notes, experiments and ideas. Guides for information I expect to maintain. Projects for longer-running projects. That gives me:
content/ ├── posts/ ├── guides/ └── projects/ I also created separate Hugo archetypes for each. Each article also gets a description and tags, everything gets a creation date, projects and guides get lastmod with projects getting active, completed, on-hold.
Below is an example for projects.
archtype/projects.md --- title: "{{ replace .File.ContentBaseName `-` ` ` | title }}" date: {{ .Date }} lastmod: {{ .Date }} draft: true description: "" tags: [] status: "active" --- A new post, guide or project can now be created with -
hugo new content posts/my-new-post.md hugo new content guides/my-new-guide.md hugo new content projects/my-new-project.md I decided not to bother with categories. The Posts, Guides and Projects sections already provide the main structure, while tags can describe what the content is actually about.
I was particularly interested in SEO, so I inspected one of the HTML files generated by Hugo.
So there didn’t appear to be any need to bolt another SEO system onto the site.
Putting the Site on GitHub Once the local site was working, I created a GitHub repository called vincatech.
I created a dedicated GitHub SSH key and configured ~/.ssh/config to use it for github.com. I then uploaded the SSH key to GitHub. The repository remote then became:
# Create the GitHub SSH key ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "github" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_github # Test GitHub authentication ssh -T git@github.com # Rename the local branch to main git branch -M main # Change the existing origin from HTTPS to SSH git remote add origin git@github.com:Vincat/vincatech.git # Push and set the upstream git push -u origin main Connecting Cloudflare to GitHub This is where things became more interesting.
To begin you need to log into your Cloudflare account then go to Computer –> Workers & Pages, click on Create Application, it is there you select GitHub, authorize the connection with read only access to the specific repo for the website.
The build command I used was:
First Gotcha: Wrangler Configuration The Hugo build worked immediately, but deployment failed with:
ERROR A compatibility_date is required when uploading a Worker. The solution was to create wrangler.jsonc in the root of the repository:
wrangler.jsonc { "name": "vincatech", "compatibility_date": "2026-08-24", "assets": { "directory": "./public/" } } Once that was committed and pushed, Cloudflare rebuilt the site.
This time Wrangler found the 87 generated files, uploaded them and successfully deployed the site.
Second Custom Domain Because the Worker itself is hosting the complete static site, vincatech.net needed to be configured as a Custom Domain.
vincatech.net as the Worker’s Custom Domain.
Third Gotcha: Old DNS The site still didn’t work from my laptop because I had some old DNS records from previous experiments, so before going down this road, I suggest clearing all DNS records. After removing the old records and allowing Cloudflare to configure the Worker custom domain, the public site started working.
Now take note that sometimes DNS propagation can take up to an hour, so if things don’t work initially then maybe it’s time to have a break and a cup of tea.
The initial setup had more traps than I expected, particularly because Cloudflare’s current Workers workflow differs from many older Hugo and Cloudflare Pages tutorials.
But now that it is configured, publishing should be little more than:
write article git add . git commit -m "Add new post" git push Cloudflare takes care of everything after that.
For a small technical blog, that’s exactly what I wanted: Markdown files on my laptop, the source safely stored in Git, static pages with virtually nothing to maintain, and no web server for me to look after.
